en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
Cīvaravagga 1.
Kathina Sikkhāpada:
Now, venerable friends, these thirty rules of expiation involving forfeiture come up for recitation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Vesālī at the Gotamaka Shrine.
Now at that time, the triple robe had been authorized by the Blessed One for the monks.

The group of six monks, thinking, “The triple robe has been authorized by the Blessed One,” entered the village with one set of the triple robe, stayed in the monastery with another set of the triple robe, and went down to bathe with yet another set of the triple robe.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks keep extra robes?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and so forth].
“Is it true, monks, that you wear extra robes?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
"How indeed, you foolish men, can you wear an extra robe?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Whosoever, however, should wear an extra robe, that is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, an extra robe had come into the possession of the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda wished to give that robe to the Venerable Sāriputta,
but the Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Sāketa.
Then, it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“The Blessed One has laid down a training rule:
‘An extra robe must not be worn. Yet this extra robe has come into my possession.”
“I wish to give this robe to the Venerable Sāriputta,
yet the Venerable Sāriputta is staying at Sāketa.
How, then, should I proceed?”
Then the Venerable Ānanda reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“But how long will it be, Ānanda, before Sāriputta arrives?
“In nine or ten days, Blessed One.”
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to keep an extra robe for at most ten days.
And thus, bhikkhus, you should recite this training rule:”

“When the robe-making season is finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, a monk may keep an extra robe for at most ten days. For one who keeps it beyond that, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
“‘When the robe-making season is finished’:
for a monk, his robe has either been made, or it has been lost, or destroyed, or burnt, or the expectation of obtaining a robe has ceased.”
"When the kaṭhina has been suspended" means:
it has been suspended by one of the eight headings of the summary, or it has been suspended prematurely by the Saṅgha.
"At most ten days" means...
It may be kept for at most ten days.
An extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) is defined as one that has neither been formally resolved upon (*anadhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned to another (*avikappita*).
"Robe" means any one of the six kinds of robes, the last of which is subject to assignment.
For one who exceeds that [limit], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.
At the rising of the sun on the eleventh day, it becomes subject to forfeiture.
It is to be forfeited to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, should it be forfeited:

That bhikkhu, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior bhikkhus, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
"Venerable sirs, this robe-cloth of mine has been kept beyond ten days and is to be forfeited;
I now forfeit it to the Saṅgha."
Having relinquished it, the offense must be confessed.
A competent and capable monk must receive the confession of the offense.
The relinquished robe must be given back.
“Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.
This robe-cloth, which was subject to forfeiture by the monk so-and-so, has been relinquished to the Sangha.
If it seems appropriate to the Sangha, let the Sangha give this robe-cloth back to the monk so-and-so.”

That bhikkhu, having approached a number of bhikkhus, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior bhikkhus, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak to them thus:
“Venerable sirs, this robe-cloth of mine has exceeded ten days and is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to you, venerable sirs.”
Having relinquished it, the offense must be confessed.
A competent and capable monk must receive the confession of the offense.
The relinquished robe-cloth must be given away.
“Venerable sirs, let my words be heard.
This robe-cloth, which is subject to relinquishment for the monk named so-and-so, has been surrendered to you, venerable sirs.
If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, may the venerable ones give this robe-cloth back to the monk named so-and-so.”

That bhikkhu, having approached another bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his haunches, and having extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak to him thus:
“Friend, this robe of mine has been kept beyond ten days and is subject to relinquishment;
I relinquish it to you, Venerable Sir.”
Having relinquished it, the offense must be confessed.
That monk must accept the offense.
The relinquished robe must be given back.
“I give this robe-cloth to the venerable one.
If ten days have passed and he perceives that ten days have passed, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If ten days have passed and he is in doubt, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If ten days have passed and he perceives that they have not passed, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If it has not been formally determined and he perceives that it has been determined, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it has not been assigned to another and he perceives that it has been assigned, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it has not been relinquished, but he perceives that it has been relinquished, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it is not lost, but he perceives that it is lost, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it is not destroyed, but he perceives that it is destroyed, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it has not been burnt, but he perceives it as burnt, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it has not been stolen, but he perceives it as stolen, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he uses a robe that should have been forfeited without having forfeited it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If ten days have not elapsed, but he perceives that they have elapsed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If ten days have not elapsed, but he is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If ten days have not elapsed, and he perceives that they have not elapsed, there is no offense.
There is no offense if,
within ten days, one resolves upon it, assigns it, gives it away, it is lost, it is destroyed, it is burnt, they take it after having stolen it, they take it on trust,
or in the case of one who is insane.
"Regarding the first offender":
Now at that time, the group of six monks did not give back robes that had been relinquished.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
(…) “Monks, a robe that has been relinquished must not be withheld.
Whoever should withhold it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The first training rule on the kaṭhina is finished.
